newsitem.title: FRANCE: France faces weighty post-holiday political choices.
newsitem.headline: France faces weighty post-holiday political choices.

text.p: France's new leftist government faces a full menu of weighty political choices on Wednesday when it returns to work following the summer holidays in the annual rite known here as "La Rentree".

Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, who came to power in June, had put off key decisions on Europe, spending, taxation and jobs to gain more time to learn more about the state of the nation's finances inherited from the previous conservative government.

Now the time has come for him to disclose how he plans to fulfil campaign promises to hold down public deficits sufficiently to launch European monetary union while creating 700,000 new jobs, preserving fragile economic growth and trimming the working week with no loss in pay.
The process begins on Wednesday when his cabinet meets for the first time since July 30, marking the first major government event of this year's Rentree.
On the agenda are proposed laws to create 350,000 jobs for young people and carry out defence reforms including a switch to an all-volunteer army.
The defence reform bill might also trigger a debate with President Jacques Chirac, who has vowed to keep the French military strong despite a reduction in troop strength.

Political analysts predict that the conservative Chirac, forced to share power with the left after calling a snap election in which he lost his centre-right majority in parliament, will warn Jospin against significant defence spending cuts in 1998.

Jospin is expected to seek major cuts in order to fund domestic needs and still meet the Maastricht Treaty requirements for the launch of a single European currency, including a public deficit target of three percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said when unveiling an audit of state finances last month that the public deficit was heading for between 3.5 and 3.7 percent of GDP this year.
He put forward a 32-billion-franc ($5.2 billion) package of corporate tax hikes and savings to bring it down by 0.4 percentage points.
Traditionally, the government virtually shuts down in August, but Strauss-Kahn remained at work throughout the month this year to help lay the groundwork for putting 1997 and 1998 finances in order.
Jospin also was in the capital during the month to make final decisions on the spending side of the budget. He worked afterward, while on holiday at the beach, on the revenue side.
The budget will be presented to the cabinet on September 24.
Trade union leaders have criticised Jospin for his go-slow approach to the problem of joblessness in a country where unemployment stands at a record 12.6 percent.
But government officials say the jobs bill to be proposed to the cabinet on Wednesday reflects the need for rapid action.
The bill is intended to create 100,000 jobs during 1998 without additional cost to the state, Employment Ministry officials said on Tuesday.

The bill's estimated price-tag is 11.9 billion to 13.8 billion francs in 1998, but the funds are to be diverted from other programmes and thus will not affect the government's pledge to meet the three per cent deficit target required for monetary union, the officials said.
